Dr. Shanda McManus lost her younger brother, Monir Hall, to gun violence in 1992. He was 20 years old. He was killed during a drive-by shooting, and his homicide has never been solved.

McManus and Hall grew up together in Philadelphia, but their paths had already started to diverge before he was killed. Hall had a short stint in the Army, became a husband and father as a teenager, and sold drugs to support his new family. McManus went to college; she got her medical degree. But as the decades passed, her grief for her brother remained. So she started writing.

In her new book, Brother Epistles, McManus writes letters to Hall, which serve as both a portrait of her brother and reflections on the conditions and consequences encountered by so many other young Black men in cities like Philadelphia. “When my brother was murdered, there was this feeling that people blamed him for his own murder, like he brought it on himself,” McManus said. “By writing the story it really helped me see all of the structural determinants that funnel young Black men like my brother toward gun violence.”

The Trace’s Mensah M. Dean spoke with McManus about her book, her motivations for writing it, and what she hopes readers will gain.

She Wrote Letters to Her Brother After He Was Killed. Now, Her Reflections Are a Memoir: In Brother Epistles, set to be released this month, Dr. Shanda McManus delves into her decades-long grief after losing her brother to a shooting, and examines the forces shaping the lives of other young Black men.

How Many Guns Are Circulating in the U.S.?: In this tally, The Trace has tried to quantify America’s civilian gun stock. This story, originally published in March 2023, was updated on June 12, 2026, to reflect the most recent data.

‘I Was Scared.’ Minneapolis Anti-Violence Workers Enter ‘Trauma Season’ Still Reeling From ICE Shootings: In the months following the city’s federal upheaval, including the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis, some outreach groups have changed how they are preparing for summer violence.

Trump’s Justice Department Is Suing Cities and States to Dismantle Gun Laws: We’re tracking the Justice Department’s investigations and lawsuits. The latest development: On June 9, the DOJ opened an investigation into the Philadelphia Police Department’s concealed carry permit revocation process.

Understanding the gun issue is key to gaining a clearer picture of America’s paradoxes. Imagining how we might solve it is essential to envisioning a country in which American ideals are more fully achieved. One person was killed and 10 others were injured in a mass shooting in Midland, Texas, on Friday. City officials confirmed that the suspected shooter is dead. [WFAA]

Friday marked 10 years since a shooter killed 49 people and wounded dozens of others in an attack on Pulse, a queer nightclub in Orlando, Florida. A decade on, survivors are still working to heal — and for some, that’s meant helping others and fighting for LGBTQ+ rights. [The 19th]

A growing number of states are passing tighter regulations around 3D-printed firearms. Just this year, Colorado, Maine, New Jersey, New York, Virginia, and Washington enacted restrictions. The measures include prohibitions on manufacturing 3D-printed guns, limits on digital distribution of gun designs, and requirements intended to stop 3D printers from being able to print guns at all. [Stateline]

It’s been a year since Minnesota State Representative Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark Hortman, were assassinated. After they were killed, Hortman’s colleagues in the House vowed to tone down their political rhetoric. That didn’t last — and some of the most heated partisan attacks there took place during debates over public safety legislation. [The Minnesota Star Tribune] As The Trace has reported, Minnesota’s gun politics mirror the nation’s divide.

The Delaware Supreme Court could revive the state’s raise-the-age law, which required residents without a concealed carry license to be at least 21 years old to purchase a firearm. A lower state court struck down the law in September 2025. [WHYY]

The Justice Department once again dropped charges against a person who was shot by federal immigration agents. Federal prosecutors had accused Juan Carlos Rodriguez Romero, a man from St. Paul, of assaulting a federal agent with his car and biting the hand of an ICE officer during his arrest. The government cited insufficient evidence in its motion for dismissal. [Minnesota Reformer]
